Most of us in Lean know how to improve a process.

We can run a Kaizen, flesh out an A3, map a value stream, and ask a solid set of 5 Whys.

But what about the other pillar?

The one we all agree matters, yet often struggle to operationalize?

Respect for People.

I'm psyched to share that I'll be delivering the keynote at the 2026 Michigan Lean Consortium Annual Conference in Muskegon, Michigan.

My keynote, 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗣𝗿𝗮𝗶𝘀𝗲 𝗣𝗮𝗿𝗮𝗱𝗼𝘅: 𝗡𝗮𝘃𝗶𝗴𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗥𝗲𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘁 𝗳𝗼𝗿 𝗣𝗲𝗼𝗽𝗹𝗲 𝗣𝗶𝗹𝗹𝗮𝗿 – 𝗛𝗼𝘄 𝗛𝗮𝗯𝗶𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝗖𝗿𝗲𝗱𝗶𝘁 𝗔𝗻𝗰𝗵𝗼𝗿𝘀 𝗛𝗶𝗴𝗵 𝗣𝗲𝗿𝗳𝗼𝗿𝗺𝗮𝗻𝗰𝗲, explores a simple but often overlooked reality:

People don't repeat what you expect. They repeat what you recognize.

When leaders consistently acknowledge contributions, give credit, and make visible what's working, they create clarity. People make better decisions. They collaborate more effectively. They solve problems sooner. Performance improves.

We'll explore the neuroscience behind why recognition works, practical ways to build it into Leader Standard Work, and how meaningful praise strengthens both culture and results.

If you've ever wondered how to bring the Respect for People pillar to life in a way that's practical, repeatable, and measurable, I'd love to see you there.

I just had one of the most rewarding experiences an author can hope for.

At the New England Society of Association Executives (NE/SAE) Annual Meeting at Margaritaville Resort Cape Cod, I had the chance to join a Book Club discussion built around 𝙋𝙞𝙘𝙩𝙪𝙧𝙚 𝙔𝙤𝙪𝙧𝙨𝙚𝙡𝙛 𝙖 𝙇𝙚𝙖𝙙𝙚𝙧. Over the past several months, this group of emerging leaders had been meeting regularly, working through the discussion prompts and assignments together.

What struck me most wasn’t just that they read the book. It was how thoughtfully they applied it.

They shared examples like:
• Using “the pause” to stay present during difficult conversations and heated meetings

• Resisting the urge to solve problems for others so people can build confidence and capability themselves (Reminds me of Billy Ray Taylor’s famous quote: “If you fight their battles, you steal their victories.”)

• Helping people understand the "why" behind change efforts.

• Moving from blanket invitations to more intentional outreach by personally inviting people and letting them know how their expertise would strengthen a panel or leadership group.

• Using self-awareness and active listening to navigate the uncertainty and complexity that come with mergers and organizational change

Listening to them connect these ideas to real leadership challenges was both educating and energizing. (I learned a whole new category of techniques to stay present).

Books are strange things. You write them alone, hoping the ideas will eventually become useful in someone else’s world. Getting to sit in a room and hear how these leaders are actively applying the concepts was an incredible reminder of why I wrote Picture Yourself a Leader in the first place.

Many thanks to Jenna Tarabelsi, QAS of PINE (Printing Industries of New England) and everyone involved in organizing the session and creating such a thoughtful learning experience. And thank you to this impressive group of leaders for your openness, insight, and generosity in sharing your takeaways.

This was a good reminder that leadership development doesn’t happen through inspiration alone. It happens through reflection, discussion, experimentation, and practice.
Lauryn Estrella Allie Orlando John Aliberti

Book research question for you:

Have you ever been praised for doing something, but the praise was vague, so you ended up repeating the wrong behavior?

Maybe a manager told you, "Great job!" after a presentation, so you doubled down on the animation, graphics, and transitions when what they actually appreciated was your simple summary matrix at the end that helped them make a decision.

Maybe a colleague said, "Nice work leading that meeting.", so you started taking charge, talking more and directing conversations. But what they actually valued was that you listened carefully and drew quieter people into the discussion.

One of the ideas I'm exploring in my next book is that praise teaches. Whether we intend it or not, people often treat praise as a clue about what matters, what is valued, and what they should do again.

The challenge is that when praise isn't specific, people can walk away with very different interpretations.

If you've experienced something like this, I'm curious:
• What was the praise?
• What did you think they meant?
• What did you repeat?
• What did they actually value?

Stories in the comments are welcome. I'll be using the insights (and potentially some anonymized examples with permission) as I continue my research.

Bring it on, and thank you!

This year we received 330 applications from thinkers, doers, healers, artists, and innovators across the country and beyond. Choosing just nine was genuinely difficult. The nine we chose are truly extraordinary.

Pradnya Cowlagi   
Here's something remarkable: Pradnya is both CEO of her own tech company and a high school student. She'll be skewering the unclear jargon that clutters the technical world — and making a sharp case for how that kind of language abuse is really about control.

Liane Davey
Author, speaker, and consultant Liane Davey is going to reframe something you thought you understood. It's not information overload that's overwhelming us — it's Thoughtload. Prepare to see your mental life in a whole new way.

Andi Hess
Hypnotherapist Andi Hess brings us a word we didn't know we needed: fracturation. Modern life is splintering our attention in ways we're only beginning to understand — and Andi is here to help us see what's happening and what we can do about it.

Kaye Kelly
Professor of Music at Berklee College of Music, international musician, and arts administrator, Kaye thrives at the intersection of arts, community, and social justice. Her talk on recovering from artistic failure will resonate far beyond the concert hall — because learning to fail well is one of the most important skills any of us can develop.

Erica Key,
What can adults learn from the way children play? Childhood play expert Erica Key has answers — and they may surprise you. Joyful, insightful, and probably a little bit fun.

Kathy Pham
Product leader, computer scientist, and founder Kathy Pham has worked across the private, nonprofit, and public sectors at the highest levels. Her question for us: Should we let AI tell our children bedtime stories? It's a deceptively simple question with profound implications.

Kishori (Kelly) Skinner 
Doula and life coach Kishori Skinner has spent her career accompanying people through life's most profound passage. What has caring for the dying taught her about living? Everything. Don't miss this one.

Elisabeth Swan
Consultant, author, and speaker Elisabeth Swan is here to untangle the praise paradox — the strange fact that we crave praise but are hardwired to give criticism. It's one of the most human of contradictions, and Elisabeth will help us navigate it.

Molly Tsongas
Dancer, somatic coach, and nature-based mindfulness guide Molly Tsongas will show us how paying attention to birds — and to nature more broadly — can lead us back to a more grounded, satisfying, and fully human life.

Do you have a "Tech Whisperer" in your organization? Someone who brings great ideas to digital life? It's tricky to walk that line between automation and human interaction, which makes experimentation vital. Justin Kenney has a great example of how to walk that line.

🔥 Hot App Review from podcast Episode 122—Or… What Happens When Praise Gets a System

This month, Tracy ORourke and I took a different route. Instead of reviewing an app, we went straight to the source—Justin Kenney—and unpacked a tool he built himself: a Praise Board inside Microsoft Teams. Why did he build it? Because people asked for a better way to recognize others. That, and he just loves a technology challenge.

Reflections on operationalizing recognition"

- You need to give people the option of remaining anonymous
- "Visible" can still be public or private
- Recognition doesn’t have to be complex to be effective
- Embedding it in tools people already use lowers resistance
- It turns “nice to do” into something closer to standard work

If you use Microsoft Teams, you could have a Praise Board too ...

She bombed in front of 100 executives.
Then she turned it into her superpower.

In her early 30s, Elisabeth Swan discovered improv comedy.
No script. 
No safety net. 
Just you, a stage, and whatever the audience throws at you.

She was also building a career in Lean Six Sigma, helping organizations solve problems and eliminate waste. On the surface, improv and process improvement seem like they belong in different zip codes.

But here's what she learned performing with ImprovBoston:
Improv IS problem solving. It just happens on stage.
You take unknown inputs. 
You build with what you're given. 
You say "yes, and" to move things forward. 
You listen, really listen, because your next move depends on it.

And the secret? 
Improv has structure. 
Rules. 
Rehearsal.
Structure sets you free.

That's also the heart of continuous improvement. 
PDSA, DMAIC, 5 Whys; they're not cages. 
They're launchpads that save you from the terror of the blank page.

So when Elisabeth led Starwood Hotels' Six Sigma transformation, 
she carried improv with her everywhere.

Then came Sardinia.
A gorgeous resort. 
Global leaders from Europe, Asia, and the Middle East. 
Four simulations running simultaneously. 
She'd been awake for 25 hours. 
Her partner was unprepared. 
A European leader torpedoed the exercise.

The simulation broke.

She was devastated. 
She'd gone from a Wall Street Journal write-up to a spectacular faceplant.

The next morning, a change management consultant dragged her out of her misery:
"Elisabeth, have you never bombed before?"
"No."
"Oh, PLEASE. Let me tell you..."
And one by one, they all shared their disasters. 
Their spectacular failures. 
Their human moments.

That day taught her something improv had been whispering all along:

Mistakes are gold.

Not because failure feels good. 
But because how fast you pivot from a misstep to a learning moment defines your trajectory.
And you can play a role in helping other people survive their faceplants.

Elisabeth worked with Starwood and Marriott for decades after that.

Years later, when a partnership collapsed at the start of COVID, those same improv muscles kicked in. 
Accept reality. 
Build with what you have. 
Keep moving forward.

She started writing weekly stories on LinkedIn. 
Sharing her faceplants. 
Drawing illustrations. 
Asking: How did YOU deal with this?

The response was overwhelming. 
It became an award-winning book (Picture Yourself a Leader). 
It opened doors to keynotes and speaking.

All from the same place improv taught her to operate: 
Say "yes, and." 
Listen deeply. 
Make others look good. 
When you fall, get back up. 
Then help the next person up, too.

When I asked Elisabeth what she wants her legacy to be, she said:

"She helped me see how capable I am.
She made learning and making mistakes fun.
She made me feel like I mattered."

After spending time with her, I believe she's already living that legacy.

Read the full conversation with Elisabeth in this month's Faceplant Files.

🤔 Have you ever considered your own useful assets? Your personal playbook? What makes you, you?

My current book assignment, "Inventory your book assets", got me going down this road. 

My homework is to list the stories, interviews, frameworks, research, failed experiments, and working ones that could make a difference.

That shifted my thinking about “assets” more broadly.

Not as something you own.
But as something you’ve created and now use intentionally, that makes a difference to you.

What’s in your personal asset inventory?
If you applied this same thinking to yourself, it might include:

🚧 Lived experiences (career moves, crashes, pivots)
📖 Stories you tell often (and why they land)
🛠️ Checklists, heuristics, or rules of thumb (90-second pause)
🤝 Collaborators who elevate your thinking (your go-to peeps)
⚡ Ways you consistently show up (curious, ready to pivot, with humor)

Most of us don’t stop to catalog these.
If we're on autopilot, we might not use them as well as we could.

Stories come first for a reason: we're storytellers from way back. If you're an instructor (and we all are at some point), you use them to teach. Stories bond the listener and the teller through mirror neurons, which is why they're so powerful.

I've consciously retired some stories. Either because I have a better one, or because I got tired of hearing it, and I challenged myself to come up with something new.

Or, a story might need fine-tuning. Anecdotes are great, but lack an arc and essential stakes. Are you telling fascinating anecdotes that could be more powerfully told as stories?

Melisa Buie, PhD, recently interviewed me for her "Faceplant Files" series (highly recommended), and THAT got me reliving some pivotal failures. She's a skilled interviewer who draws out the role of faceplants in making us US. As Karen Martin can attest, it's a profoundly moving experience.

Got me thinking!

❓ What's a personal asset you've got that deserves more attention?

👋 How critical is remembering names? I remember my chiropractor’s dog’s name, “Tibby,” by associating it with the tibia (assuming that's part of anatomy studies). Remembering a dog’s name might not matter that much (Depends on the person … and the dog), yet having a way to remember people’s names is key for a slew of reasons.

First, don’t berate yourself if you’re bad with names—we all are. Mainly because proper nouns get way less brain attention. Fifty percent of our brain’s processing is devoted to vision, so we’re far more interested in faces.

It’s worth developing techniques for storing names since both remembering and forgetting a person’s name—or mispronouncing it—have an immediate impact on a person and, by extension, organizational culture.

When people hear their names, they tune right in (think back to the chill of hearing a parent pronounce your full name—that got your attention). On the flip side, forgetting someone’s name triggers a feeling of exclusion and a sense of being unimportant. Not a good way to foster engagement and collaboration.

I know of a company with 1,200 employees where the CEO knows every person’s name. That tells you a lot about that culture without even knowing what they do. It also illuminates the role of intention in remembering names. 

My husband—self-proclaimed “bad-with-names” spouse—could remember everyone’s drinks when he was a bartender. His recall was so good that, after being rear-ended, he looked into the rearview mirror and called out, “Whisky Sour!” upon recognizing the driver. Both he and the CEO remembered because they wanted to—it was important to them.

Want to remember? A few tips:

👂Receive: Introductions can be full of distraction so focus when people say their name—easier said than done.

🔁 Repeat: Say the person’s name once or twice when you’re introduced to give your brain a shot at remembering—repetition is fundamental to retention.

🧠 Relate: Since names are contextless, give them context. “Ben” is a big guy, and “Big Ben” is memorable (the association can be random, quirky, and nonsensical, which is okay since you’ll never share it!).

✍️ Record: Write it down if you can. I just discovered that one of my clients took on a rescue donkey named Gladys to protect her baby goats from coyotes. What? There is no way I want to forget about Gladys.

Remembering names isn’t about talent—it’s about intention. And intention, repeated, becomes culture. If a CEO can know 1,200 names, and a bartender can remember every drink, the rest of us probably aren’t “bad with names.” We’re just deciding what matters.

Dogs? Donkeys? That’s a perfect segue to remind you that there’s more of these leadership topics and tips in The Swan Dive—the monthly newsletter that explores how to build high-performance habits. Join me in the deep end.😊

items.content:
🏀 Metrics are tricky because for good or ill—they drive behavior. What about the balance of individual versus team metrics? Or team versus organizational? What about metrics that capture effort versus focusing only on “wins”?

My family-induced obsession with basketball has me immersed in individual and team metrics. Sports provide an abundance of analogies because they’re so stat-heavy. When comparing their metric saturation to that of the business world, they’re more like call centers with hold times, abandonment rates, and resolution rates, etc. There’s much to learn from hoops.

The most obvious basketball stat is buckets made, yet the NBA and the WNBA have developed ways to capture effort. Basketball stats have evolved to capture collaboration and the overall impact of each team member, as opposed to simply the number of baskets they make. There are rebounds (efforts that get your team the ball), assists (efforts to that led to a teammate scoring), blocks (efforts that keep the opponent from scoring), and, added in 2007, the confounding “+/-” score for each player.

The +/- is controversial stat that apparently has early roots in the NHL and was originally called “The Team Contribution Index” or TCI. The idea grew as coaches and players tried to get at the impact of a player that wasn’t captured in standard metrics. The way they set screens, whether they hustled on defense, passes they made that weren’t assists, along with their leadership and playmaking. 

AI Definition: The plus/minus (+/-) score in basketball measures a player's impact on the game by calculating the net difference between their team's points scored and allowed while they are on the court. A positive number (+10) means the team outscored the opponent during their time, while a negative number (-5) indicates they were outscored. Pretty straightforward.

I hear arguments for and against the +/- stat. Some point out that it’s a helpful aggregate score, rather than looking at individual games. I’m not QUITE as steeped in this to argue for or against it, I just appreciate that they’re trying to capture the whole player. If you focus mainly on baskets made, then you are encouraging what they call “iso” or isolation play. Meaning, if the main metric is baskets made, then I’m focused on getting myself to the basket. 

There are endless reports of star players hitting new highs in points, yet the team still loses. But if you focus on a balance of metrics that include effort and impact, then the player is more likely to focus on helping their teammates and the team. 

Unlike the NBA, we can’t watch film or count assists, and it’s unclear how to translate the +/- to the business world, yet we need better effort metrics because they drive good team behavior and therefore benefit the institution as a whole.

I got to see the river otter peek his head out of the ice this morning. Adorable? Yes, but I’m relaying this as part of a “causal gratitude” experiment. 

You may already have a practice of writing down 3 things you’re grateful for at the start or end of a day, and if so, you’re probably aware that counting your blessings makes you a happier person. What you may NOT know is that you can experience longer-lasting positivity and resilience if you include the root cause of the thing you’re grateful for.

A new study from American Psychologist characterizes the classic “List-3-things” approach as passive. As if you’re simply the lucky recipient of great stuff that happens to you, whereas the reality is that you’ve generally had a hand in those things. This reminds me of the quote, “You make your own luck” (generally attributed to a string of luminaries stretching from country-singing legend Loretta Lynn to Roman Philosopher Seneca). 

Based on the neurological research, you get more impact if you not only note the thing you’re grateful for, “The vendor just reduced their prices”, but you also reflect on the cause, “because I spent time and effort on maintaining a good relationship." Seemingly subtle, but it changes things. 

🧪 Results of the Experiment:
I spent last week adapting my morning habit to reflect “causal” gratitude, and the experience has been mixed. It takes longer, since you have to sit with the cause for a second, and you might not be able to connect it. The example of the otter was fairly straightforward:

“I’m got to see the river otter stick his head out of the ice this morning because I made it a point to live on a pond and put my desk in front of a window.”

Other attempts felt a strangely self-congratulatory:

“I got to have fabulous coconut chicken curry last night because I married a great cook.”

In general, the practice forced me to own my part in what’s going well. It puts the Gratitude Practice slightly more adjacent to the Small Wins Practice (big fan). And, no surprise, that rewires your brain in a good way as well. So far, it’s a keeper.

If you’re interested in a less-stressed, more positive brain, try it out. What are you grateful for, and what do you suspect is the cause?

Which begs the question, where are we accepting defaults that fail to serve us? Apps drive a lot of it these days, so that’s a good place to start.

⏰ Another software-influenced default is the 1-hour meeting. It’s taken a few bold contrarians to declare 45- or 50-minute time slots as their norm. It still takes extra steps to alter the built-in 1-hour session, yet the practical and physiological realities beg for change:

- Calendars stacked with back-to-back meetings leave zero time for reflection, action, regrouping, preparation … and the list goes on.

- Cognitive neuroscience suggests the brain needs to switch tasks or rest frequently. The "50-minute rule" (ending meetings at 50 minutes) allows for decent cognitive breaks

I recently engaged a coach, and was immediately impressed when she announced that we’d be meeting for 50-minute sessions. We’ve only spoken once, yet this one construct made me think more of her. There are folks who offer 25- or 45-minute meetings on their calendar apps, so there’s a way to change that default. Yet most situations require extra steps.

Switching focus, we've also established some non-software-driven habits that may no longer serve us.

- Holding meetings when an email-update would suffice
Engaging in lengthy email exchanges when a phone call would be faster (using the rule of 3 helps—once there are 3 emails about a topic, time to pick up the phone)

These are defaults that warrant scrutiny, since even when we know better, it’s not easy to resist the thing in front of us. Some ways of operating seem easier, even though a bit of scrutiny proves us wrong. And some of our assumptions seem inevitable, although they’re not:

1️⃣ Who is your MVP for?
↳ Define your ideal customer before you build anything.
↳ What single problem are you solving, and how does it provide immediate value?

2️⃣ Validate the problem first
↳ Would people actually pay for a solution to this?
↳ If nobody is eager, rethink before you write a line of code.

3️⃣ The Core MVP Rules

✅ Solve one specific problem in the simplest way possible.
✅ Be usable without extensive training.
✅ Provide immediate value.
✅ Be built in 4 to 8 weeks maximum.
❌ Don't build the full product vision from day one.
❌ Don't pack in features nobody asked for.

4️⃣ Get Your First Users
↳ Social media, early access deals, direct email outreach.
↳ Your first users are your best product team. Treat them that way.

5️⃣ The Feedback Loop
↳ Launch. Get feedback. Iterate. Relaunch.
↳ Remove what isn't working before you add anything new.

6️⃣ Signs Your MVP Is Ready to Scale: 

✅ Strong retention and repeat users.
✅ Users asking for more features.
✅ Customers willing to pay without being pushed.

If in doubt, aim to remove as many things as you can.

The simplest version that delivers real value will always teach you more than the most complete version you could imagine.

Those platforms aren't just crawling your site. 

They're evaluating your entire digital footprint, 
Including reviews, community presence, third-party mentions, and entity data.

The brands winning AI search are building that ecosystem now. 

Here's what you need to secure your visibility now: 

1️⃣ AI platforms
↳ ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Perplexity, Copilot, Grok and AI Overviews.
↳ Buyers are going here first, but it's what feeds them that matters. 

2️⃣ Review platforms
↳ Trustpilot, G2, Capterra, Tripadvisor.
↳ Reviews are one of the strongest trust signals in AI search.

3️⃣ Community platforms
↳ Reddit, Quora, industry forums.
↳ AI pulls from real community discussions. AI knows that people trust people.

4️⃣ Content platforms
↳ YouTube, LinkedIn, Substack, industry blogs and publications.
↳ Publishing is the new go-to to demonstrate expertise and topical relevance.

5️⃣ Entity platforms
↳ Wikipedia, Wikidata, Crunchbase.
↳ AI systems look here to understand who you are and what you do. 

6️⃣ Authority and validation
↳ Gartner, industry publications, third-party press.
↳ AI looks for external validation over self-promotion. 

7️⃣ Search and discovery
↳ Google, Bing, Google Business Profile.
↳ Strong SEO is the foundation and makes AI citations faster.

The race is no longer for the best, most optimised website. 

Now you need to establish the strongest ecosystem around your brand.
